title: SOLID, coupling and cohesion
subtitle: Learn what coupling, cohesion and the five SOLID principles really say, and when following them blindly makes code harder to change.

c.v: This story is made up, but both halves are common. Kiran's team runs the checkout service of a shoe store. The
Checkout
class creates an
SmtpMailer
and calls it to send order emails. Refunds and sign-ups do the same.

Then the company moved to an HTTP email API. The new client took different arguments. Kiran had to edit checkout, refunds and sign-up. Each change needed new tests and a new deploy. Worse, the checkout tests had always opened a real SMTP connection, so they were slow and often failed in
CI
A new tech lead said, "We need SOLID." The team added an interface in front of every class.
OrderService
got
IOrderService
PriceCalculator
got
IPriceCalculator
. Six months later there were 60 interfaces, each with exactly one implementation.
Now a new developer had to jump through two files for every call. The vendor problem was solved, but adding a field to an order touched more files than before.
The first design had too much
coupling
. The second added layers that hid nothing. Both made change slow.
In the
deep modules lesson
, you learned to hide each hard decision behind a small interface. This lesson gives you the older words for the same goal, and five popular rules built on them.

In 1974, Stevens, Myers and Constantine published "Structured design" in the IBM Systems Journal. They called coupling "the measure of the strength of association established by a connection from one module to another".
Strong coupling makes a module harder to understand, change or fix on its own. They advised "the weakest possible coupling between modules".
Fewer connections also mean fewer paths for changes and errors to spread. The paper calls these "ripple" effects.
Kiran's vendor change was one.
The second idea is
cohesion
. The paper called it cohesiveness, measured by "binding": how strongly the parts inside one module belong together.
You lower coupling in two ways at once: fewer links between modules, and stronger links inside each one.
Their weakest kind is "coincidental" binding, where the parts have no real relationship.
The key idea.
Put things that change together in one place. Keep things that change for different reasons apart. SOLID gives five more specific rules that serve this goal, and each one can be overdone.
SOLID names five principles that Robert C. Martin teaches:
single responsibility
open-closed
Liskov substitution
interface segregation
and
dependency inversion
He links his single responsibility principle back to Parnas and to Constantine's coupling and cohesion.
Step through the vendor change in two designs. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
S: single responsibility
Martin states SRP as "each software module should have one and only one reason to change".
He says the reasons are people: "It is people who request changes."
His short form is: "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons. Separate those things that change for different reasons."
Misreading:
"a class should do one thing", so every method gets its own class. That is not how Martin defines it. Ousterhout calls small classes taken to the extreme
classitis
In their debate, he says the related "One Thing" rule for methods "is simply wrong in many cases".
O: open-closed
Martin quotes Bertrand Meyer's 1988 book: a module is open if it is "available for extension", and closed if it is "available for use by other modules".
Martin reads this as plugins: high-level policy stays apart from low-level detail.
A new discount is a new
PriceRule
. You do not edit
finalPrice
Misreading:
"never edit old code", or "add plug-in points everywhere". You cannot guess every future change. An extension point that nobody uses is cost with no benefit.
L: Liskov substitution
Liskov and Wing argue that subtyping is about behaviour. Objects of the subtype should behave like the supertype "as far as anyone or any program using supertype objects can tell."
Any property you can prove about type T should also hold for a subtype S.
Their example: a stack and a queue can both have
put
and
get
. The type checker may accept either. But code written for a stack is unlikely to work with a queue.
In the code below,
PaymentGateway
promises that
refund
returns the money to the customer.
Misreading:
"the subclass compiles, so it is fine". Type checking catches only a small part of correctness.
Martin's short form: a program that uses an interface "must not be confused by an implementation of that interface."
I: interface segregation
Martin's line: "Keep interfaces small so that users don't end up depending on things they don't need."
The gift card fix is two small interfaces:
Misreading:
one method per interface, everywhere. Split by what each caller needs, not by method count.
D: dependency inversion
Martin's line: "High level modules should not depend upon low level details."
Schuchert adds: capture low-level dependencies in domain-relevant abstractions.
The interface speaks the orders language,
orderPlaced
, not
sendSmtp(host, port, mime)
Misreading:
"dependency inversion means a DI framework". The last line is
dependency injection
. Schuchert puts it this way: "DI is about how one object acquires a dependency." In his summary, "DI is about wiring, IoC is about direction, and DIP is about shape."
You can inject a concrete class and gain nothing. He also warns that "all abstractions have a cost".
Connascence: finer words for coupling
Connascence
is "a taxonomy for different types of coupling".
It judges each case by strength, degree (how many things are involved) and locality (how far apart they are).
For example, connascence of position means two parts "must agree on the order of values". Reading fields by name instead makes the coupling weaker.
The critiques
Dan North's CUPID started as a light-hearted challenge to SOLID. At first he wanted to replace each principle with something more useful.
He gives an example: splitting a report's content from its format, as SRP is often explained, "creates artificial seams" when both change together.
He prefers properties to principles: "Principles are like rules: you are either compliant or you are not."
In 2020, Martin answered a reader who cited North's views on SOLID. He wrote that North's slides "completely miss the point" of SRP.
He called North's "Just write simple code" good advice. But he added that "simplicity requires disciplines guided by principles."
Read both, then judge each rule by one test: does it make the next real change smaller?
Call a concrete class directly
, while it is stable.
Vendor or I/O changes ripple into callers.
The detail is stable and in your own code.
Interface owned by the caller, injected
Swap details in one wiring line.
One more name. A small design effort.
The detail is a vendor, I/O, or needs a fake in tests.
Interface for every class
Each change touches two files.
Shallow layers, more jumping between files.
Rarely. Remove ones with one implementation and no test fake.
Split a class by reason to change
Each group's change stays in one place.
More classes to name.
Different people ask for different changes.
Split until each class does "one thing"
Code that changes together is spread out.
Classitis.
Rarely.

c.v: For a class under review, ask: "Who asks for changes to this?" Two different answers suggest a split. One answer suggests keeping it together.
Before adding an interface, name the second implementation or the test fake. If you cannot, wait.
Put interfaces next to the code that uses them, in its language.
OrderNotifier
belongs to orders, not to the email package.
In code review, look for
throw new Error("not supported")
in an implementation. It usually means a broken substitution or an interface that is too big. See
reviewing code
Keep the wiring of concrete classes in one place, such as
main
. Then a vendor change is one line.
When a change touches many files, write down which coupling caused it. Add it to your
tech debt
list.
"List every place where business code creates or calls this vendor client directly. For each, show the arguments that are specific to the vendor."
"Find interfaces in this repo with exactly one implementation. For each, say whether any test uses a fake for it."
"Find classes that implement an interface but throw 'not supported' or do nothing in some methods. Explain which callers could break."
The agent did not add an interface and an
Impl
class for every class to "follow SOLID".
New interfaces use the caller's words, not the vendor's method names.
A suggested split groups code by who asks for changes, not by method count.
Behaviour did not change. Run the tests before and after. The
testing strategy lesson
shows where fakes help.
Before this:
complexity and deep modules
. Next:
testing strategy
, where these seams make tests fast. Later lessons on design patterns, clean and hexagonal architecture, and low-level object-oriented design build on this one. Related:

and

q.v: An Invoice class computes the total, renders a PDF and saves itself to the database. Finance, design and the DBA team all ask for changes to it. What does SRP suggest?

options.v: Split it so each method lives in its own class.
Split it along the three reasons to change, so each group's changes stay in one place.
Leave it, because it is about one thing, invoices.

why.v: Martin defines SRP by reasons to change, which are people. Split by those reasons, not by method count.

q.v: A GiftCardGateway implements PaymentGateway, but its refund method always throws "not supported". PaymentGateway promises that refunds work. The code compiles. Which principle does it break?

options.v: Liskov substitution, because callers of PaymentGateway can no longer rely on refund working.
Open-closed, because the class was modified.

why.v: Liskov and Wing say a subtype must behave as its supertype promises. Matching types is not enough.

q.v: What is the difference between dependency inversion and dependency injection?

options.v: They are two names for the same thing.
Injection is about how an object gets its dependency. Inversion is about the shape of the interface and who owns it.
Inversion needs a framework. Injection does not.

why.v: In Schuchert's summary, "DI is about wiring" and "DIP is about shape".

q.v: Your codebase has 60 interfaces. Each one has exactly one class that implements it, and no test uses a fake. What is the likely problem?

options.v: Shallow layers that add names without hiding anything.

why.v: An interface with one implementation and no second user often hides nothing. Ousterhout warns that too many small, shallow classes add complexity.
